questions.question_text: A person records a BAC of $0.06$. Use $\text{Time} = \dfrac{\text{BAC}}{0.015}$ to calculate the number of hours required for their BAC to drop to zero.

options.why: Multiplied $0.06$ by $0.015$ instead of dividing.
Divided by $0.024$ instead of the standard rate $0.015$.
Divided by $0.01$ instead of $0.015$.

questions.question_text: A driver tested at a roadside checkpoint records a BAC of $0.035$. Calculate the time required for their BAC to reach zero, in hours and minutes.

options.why: Treated $0.333\ldots\text{ hours}$ as $33\text{ minutes}$ instead of multiplying by $60$.
Treated the decimal $0.035$ as $35$ minutes.
Divided by $0.02$ instead of the standard metabolic rate of $0.015$.

questions.question_text: A driver stops drinking at $11{:}30\text{ pm}$ with a BAC of $0.045$. At what clock time will their BAC reach zero?

options.why: Calculated $2\text{ hours}$ instead of $3\text{ hours}$.
Added $3.5\text{ hours}$ instead of $3.0\text{ hours}$.
Divided by $0.01$ to get $4.5\text{ hours}$.

questions.question_text: A $75\text{ kg}$ male consumes $5$ standard drinks over $3\text{ hours}$. Calculate how long he must wait after drinking stops for his BAC to reach zero, to the nearest minute.

options.why: Used the female formula constant ($5.5$) instead of the male constant ($6.8$) to calculate BAC.
Calculated the total time from when drinking began instead of the waiting time after drinking stops.
Used $0.02$ as the hourly metabolic rate instead of $0.015$.

questions.question_text: A person's BAC took $5\text{ hours } 20\text{ minutes}$ to decrease to zero. What was their BAC when drinking stopped?

options.why: Treated $5\text{ hours } 20\text{ minutes}$ as $5.2\text{ hours}$.
Rounded $5.333$ hours down to $5.0$ hours.
Divided the hours by $0.015$ instead of multiplying.

questions.question_text: A person has a BAC of $0.072$. Calculate the time required for their BAC to reach zero, in hours and minutes.

options.why: Treated $0.8$ hours as $8$ minutes instead of multiplying by $60$.
Rounded $4.8$ hours to $4.5$ hours.
Divided $0.078$ by $0.015$ due to a transcription error.

questions.question_text: A Provisional driver finishes drinking at $10{:}15\text{ pm}$ with a BAC of $0.057$. What is the earliest time the next morning they can legally drive ($0.00$ limit)?

options.why: Rounded $3.8\text{ hours}$ to $3\text{ hours } 40\text{ minutes}$.
Treated $3.8\text{ hours}$ as $3\text{ hours } 80\text{ minutes}$.
Calculated time to reach $0.02$ rather than zero BAC.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{Time} = \dfrac{0.057}{0.015} = 3.8\text{ hours} = 3\text{ hours } 48\text{ minutes}$
$10{:}15\text{ pm} + 3\text{ h } 48\text{ min} = 2{:}03\text{ am}$

questions.question_text: A $60\text{ kg}$ female drinks $4$ standard drinks over $3\text{ hours}$. Calculate the total time in hours and minutes (to the nearest minute) from when she started drinking until her BAC drops to zero.

options.why: Calculated only the sobering time after drinking stopped, omitting the $3\text{ hours}$ of drinking.
Used the male formula constant ($6.8$) to find BAC.
Omitted the metabolism term $7.5H$ from the BAC formula.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{BAC} = \dfrac{10(4) - 7.5(3)}{5.5(60)} = \dfrac{17.5}{330} \approx 0.05303$
$\text{Time to zero} = \dfrac{0.05303}{0.015} \approx 3.535\text{ h} = 3\text{ h } 32\text{ min}$
$\text{Total time} = 3\text{ h} + 3\text{ h } 32\text{ min} = 6\text{ hours } 32\text{ minutes}$
